idiom_name: noexcept friend/member swap plus std::swap / the Swappable requirement
implementation_notes: C++11 absorbed most of the idiom: std::swap is conditionally noexcept - noexcept(is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T> && is_nothrow_move_assignable_v<T>) - and since C++17 that specification is std::is_nothrow_swappable_v<T>, so a type with nothrow move operations gets a non-throwing exchange without writing anything. The personalized form is a two-line friend swap that exchanges the handles and is marked noexcept, which also makes the Swappable named requirement testable; the C++03 three-part protocol (member swap, namespace-scope swap, std::swap specialization) collapses into the friend function because unqualified calls find it by ADL while std::swap reaches it through the customization rules. Write it whenever the default would copy resource-owning members instead of exchanging one handle (pimpl classes with user-declared copy operations, containers with custom allocators, COW handles) and whenever copy-and-swap assignment needs a guarantee it can name.
pitfalls: Declaring a copy constructor or copy assignment (as pimpl classes do) suppresses the implicit move operations, so std::swap silently falls back to three copies and is no longer noexcept - default the moves or supply the friend swap.

noexcept is a promise, not a check: if the exchanged members can throw (a std::function, a container whose swap allocates with an unequal allocator, a user type without nothrow moves) any escape calls std::terminate; keep the swap limited to nothrow-movable handles.

Only full specializations of std::swap are legal for user types; for class templates rely on ADL with `using std::swap; swap(a, b);` at the call site, because an overload added to namespace std is undefined behaviour and may simply not be picked up.
swap(x, x) must stay a no-op: hand-rolled implementations that clear one side before assigning it back corrupt the object when both references alias.

variants.name: classic ADL swap protocol over a pimpl handle (C++03)
variants.idiom_name: member swap + namespace-scope swap + std::swap specialization
variants.implementation_notes: Before move semantics, std::swap copied (three copies, each of which could throw), so this protocol was the only way to get an efficient, exception-safe exchange: declare a public member swap that exchanges the pimpl pointer, add a non-member swap in the class's namespace so unqualified calls find it by Koenig lookup, and - for non-template classes - a full specialization of std::swap for callers that write std::swap explicitly. Copy assignment then reads `String tmp(s); tmp.swap(*this); return *this;` and the temporary's destructor releases the old resources, which is the copy-and-swap idiom. Keep the three declarations in sync: the compiler will not tell you when one is missing, and generic code silently falls back to the copy-based std::swap, which is both slower and throwing.
pitfalls: Full specialization of std::swap is only legal for user-defined types; for class templates an overload in namespace std is undefined behaviour (the Wikibooks page documents this dilemma), so template classes must rely on ADL and callers must write `using std::swap; swap(a, b);`.
C++03 has no noexcept: the guarantee is a comment or an empty throw() specification that neither the compiler nor generic code checks.
Missing any one of the three declarations silently degrades callers to the copy-based std::swap, which can throw in exactly the rollback path the idiom was introduced to protect.

variants.name: atomic exchange of a single state handle (concurrent publication)
variants.idiom_name: std::atomic exchange of one state pointer (std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> in C++20)
variants.implementation_notes: When the state is read by many threads and replaced by one writer, the non-throwing exchange becomes an atomic one: hold the whole state behind a single pointer or reference and publish it with std::atomic<T*>::exchange, or - since C++20 - std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>>::exchange so the old state is released safely once the last reader is done. Only one handle can be exchanged atomically (two independent atomics cannot be swapped as a pair), so everything that must change together has to live behind that one handle; readers then see either the old or the new state, never a half-installed one. This is the concurrent realization of "the commit step cannot fail": the fallible work builds a new immutable state, the exchange publishes it.
pitfalls: An atomic exchange publishes one reference; state split across two atomics can still be observed torn by readers, so everything that must be consistent belongs behind the single handle.
std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> is C++20 only and is not guaranteed to be lock-free; before C++20 use a raw atomic pointer with an explicit reclamation scheme or the shared_ptr atomic free functions.
exchange() is not a compare-and-swap: concurrent writers overwrite each other's state, so use compare_exchange_* when a lost update must be detected rather than silently dropped.
